eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36533/97) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been denied a fair trial in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 10 October 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr H. Brown, a lawyer practising in Ruislip, Middlesex. A man named Willi Smolny flew from Brazil to London via Copenhagen. He had with him a black suitcase containing 18 kilograms of cocaine. Thierry and Mr Terrasson were arrested by customs officers at Heathrow. The two men were carrying two similar-looking suitcases, which customs officers found to contain cocaine. Both men were charged with possession with intent to sell or smuggle the drug. They were released on bail, but a third man, Armand, who had not travelled with them, was arrested at the airport in Los Angeles. The case is described as 'one of the worst drug busts in the history of Britain' Armand Terrasson, who was on his way to Antwerp, was arrested at Heathrow. He claimed to have taken his own, not Mr Smolny’s, black suitcase from the carousel. He said that he had travelled alone to Copenhagen, taking with him a black suitcase, to meet a married woman friend. He was unable to meet her because her husband was home, so he returned immediately to London. The prosecution case was that Armand had organised the importation, using MrSmolny as the courier from Brazil to Copenhagen and London. He had instructed Mr Terrass on, with Thierry as ‘minder’, to collect Mr Smalny's suitcase as if in mistake for his own. All four defendants pleaded not guilty and gave evidence. The applicants maintained that Armand worked principally as a jewel trader, but that he did not keep written records because he systematically avoided paying taxes and duties in Brazil. The illegality of his jewel trading had motivated their lies during their initial interviews with customs officers. The defence centred around a dispute between Armand and a rival jewel trader based in Brazil called Rudi Steiner. They claimed that, in order to avoid repaying his debt, he had arranged falsely to implicate them in the importation of cocaine. But they had no evidence to connect Mr Steiner to Mr Molny’s suitcase full of drugs or to substantiate the suggestion he was a Customs and Excise informer. Brazilian businessman Steiner sent a representative across the world to deliver diamonds worth thousands of dollars in exchange for a sample of the diamonds. Steiner's representative was caught with 18 kilos of cocaine in a suitcase that was identical to the one used in the arrest of Morgan. He believed the diamonds were antiques and works of art, but the drugs were actually cocaine. The diamonds were intended to be sold in a London jewellery store, but they were used to pay for Smolny's flight and hotel stay in Denmark and the return journey to London. The cocaine was intended for the British Customs Service, but Steiner set them up in order to get them to believe they were carrying antiques, he says. The jury convicted the applicants and Mr Terrasson of importing the cocaine. Mr Smolny was acquitted. In spring 1994 the applicants learned from the French press that a Swiss undercover police officer, Commissioner Cattaneo, had written a report. In early 1995 the applicants’ solicitor obtained a copy of the report. It mentioned Rudi Steiner, describing him as one of three regular informers of the Brazilian, Danish and French police. He was said to have an interest in stolen jewels and a long-term involvement in the traffic from Brazil to Europe of large quantities of cocaine, which he was able freely to obtain from the Brazilian police. The applicants added a further ground of appeal coupled with an application for leave to call fresh evidence. They maintained that the Mato Grosso Report substantiated their suggestion at trial that Mr Steiner had access both to stolen jewels and cocaine. In their submission, the fact that the jury had not had before it evidence relating to these matters, and the judge, ignorant of the true facts, rendered their convictions unsafe. The applicants objected to the holding of an ex parte hearing, in writing on 27 November 1995 and orally before the Court of Appeal on 7 December 1995, submitting inter alia that the court was a tribunal of both fact and law and could be adversely influenced by material which was wrong. The applicants' solicitor was able to obtain a number of documents relating to the Italian proceedings. These included transcripts of interviews with Mr Steiner, arrest warrants and a list of his previous convictions. He also obtained a statement from Commissioner Cattaneo, the Swiss police officer who had prepared the Mato Grosso Report. In his statement the Commissioner confirmed the authenticity of the report. He stated that he had been introduced to Mr. Steiner by a Danish police officer and had become Mr Steiners’ “handler”, passing information to the British authorities. According to the Commissioner’s statement, his British “contact” had been a customs officer named Martin Crago, whom he had contacted at the British Embassy in Brasilia. Court of Appeal ruled that justice did not require disclosure by the Crown of the public interest immunity evidence. Court of Appeal dismissed the application for leave to appeal on 20 February 1997. 'Little, if any, of the material [put before the applicants’ counsel] would have been admissible at the trial,' the court said. 'Much of it is wholly irrelevant to the central issue in this case, namely whether British Customs and Excise officers conspired with Steiner to ‘frame’ the Atlans' 'Steiner. denied that he had been Commissioner Cattaneo’s contact and declined to answer any question about Mr Steiner. Prosecuting counsel suggested that the only way Steiner could have been sure of achieving such an end would have been to persuade the officers to ‘plant’ the drug on, or falsely attribute it to, Thierry or Terrasson. There are also a number of other questions indicating the impossibility of the Atlans’ defence. Why, if they thought they were to collect diamonds from Steiner, not drugs, did they check their luggage onto the return flight without apparently enquiring by telephone why he had not turned up or whether he had been delayed? Why did Smolny make indirect telephone contact with someone on Armand’s telephone number in Brazil on the day of the importation? Prosecuting counsel's submission provides a logical and complete answer to the complaint based on Steiner’s alleged role as an informer and drug smuggler. His only possible line of defence, though, for the reasons we have given, is a wholly unrealistic one. The evidence against them, which had been thoroughly and robustly tested at the trial, was overwhelming. Their involvement in the high value and high risk activity of drug smuggling, not some black market dealing in gems under Brazilian law, was clear. Whatever Steiner's possible role, the Atlans’ guilty participation in cocaine smuggling is clear. ...”

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30054/96) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants, next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Loughgall on 8 May 1987, alleged that their relatives had been kill unjustifiably. They invoked Articles 2, 6, 14 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Jordan v. the United UK ( no. 24746/94) and McKerr v the United. Kingdom (No. 28883/95) The application was made to the Human Rights Commission on 23 March 2000. A hearing took place in public on 4 April 2000. The applicants accepted that the summaries below are an accurate reflection of the written statements made by the official personnel involved, without making any admission as to the credibility, consistency and veracity of these statements. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Korff. The application was declared admissible by a decision of 4 April2000. The court ruled that the application was admissible and dismissed the Government's objections. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights. The RUC station, which operated on a part-time basis only, was opened as normal at 9 a.m. on 8 May 1987. Soldiers O, P, Q and R were instructed to position themselves in a wooded area to the south of the Loughgall Road, near what is known as Ballygasey Cottage. Soldiers S, T and U were positioned to the rear of St Luke’s Church. Three armed men who said they were from the IRA entered the house of the Mackle family in Aghinlig Upper, Dungannon. At about 6.30 p.m., a vehicle pulled up outside and a fourth man arrived. It appears that a bomb containing 300 to 400 pounds of explosives was prepared in the yard of the house. A blue Hiace van came from the Loughgall direction and parked outside the station. A man, dressed in blue overalls and wearing a balaclava, emerged from the rear of the van. He raised his rifle and began to shoot at the RUC station. Soldiers A to E, who had positioned themselves at windows on the first floor of the station began to return fire without warning. Soldier B received a facial injury from flying glass after a window by which he was standing was broken by gunfire. One of the IRA men drove the digger through the front gate and Soldier B, having spotted this, fired a short burst at the driver. The digger stopped and shortly afterwards there was an explosion. Soldiers A, B, D and E moved towards the front of the RUC station and continued to fire at the men near the van. Constables B and C were led outside by Constable A and Soldier C, who administered first aid to them. Soldier F also left the station by the rear and did not take any part in the shooting. Some of the soldiers stated that they came under fire. Shortly after the bomb exploded, Soldiers K and R observed what they thought was a gunman lying in the grass behind the police station. He failed to stand up when challenged to do so, and both soldiers fired several rounds at what turned out to be a large lump of wood. The bodies were wearing blue boiler suits except where specified otherwise. The first body (Patrick Kelly) was found lying on his back still moving. There were two significantly bullet damaged vehicles, a blue Toyota Hiace van (with approximately 125 bullet holes in the bodywork) and a white Citroen car. In the vicinity of the junction of Clovenden Road/Ballygasey Road there were bullet damaged Vauxhall Cavalier and Ford estate cars. Other vehicles near the scene of the attack included a red Sierra 15 metres from position 6, occupied by a woman and her daughter. A blue Escort about 70 metres from the scene which was empty. Post mortem examination revealed at least a dozen wounds to the torso and head. Pathologist observed at least twenty separate missile wounds (i.e. bullet and fragment) and found that discharge abrasion on an entry wound on the front of the neck indicated that when the gun was discharged the muzzle was within several feet of the body. There were four loaded rifles and one shotgun found in the van. Three of the stocks were folded. The sixth body (Eugene Kelly), which had massive head damage and multiple injuries elsewhere, was seated in the driver seat. There was a revolver lying between the driver’s seat and his door. The seventh body (Declan Arthurs) was lying in a lane-way opposite the premises of the Loughgall Football Club. The police took possession of the firearms used by Soldiers A to X. In total, 678 spent cartridge cases were recovered, 78 of which were from IRA weapons. Two forensic doctors carried out post mortem examinations of the bodies. The RUC forwarded a report to the Director of Public Prosecutions for Northern Ireland (the DPP) on the outcome of their RUC investigation. On 22 September 1988, he concluded that the evidence did not warrant the prosecution of any person involved in the shootings. Judgments were given by the Court of Appeal on 6 December 1990 and by the House of Lords on 22 September 1990. The inquest was adjourned on 24 September 1990, pending the determination of the Devine case, which concerned the powers of Coroners and the procedure at inquests. The inquest into the deaths of the three men was held on 30 May 1995 in public before a Coroner and a jury of 10 members. The RUC and Ministry of Defence were represented. The Coroner made available the maps and photographs but did not permit counsel (other than those instructed on the Coroner’s behalf) to see witness statements until the witness was giving evidence. On the same day of the inquest, counsel for the six families asked for the proceedings to be adjourned to allow them to seek judicial review of the decision to refuse access to the witness statements. This step was taken on 31 May 1995 following consultation with the families. The family of Declan Arthurs sought judicial review of the Coroner’s decisions not to allow the legal representatives to see witness statements before they gave evidence. The judge placed considerable emphasis on the character of an inquest as a fact finding exercise and not a method of apportioning guilt. It was concluded on 2 June 1995 that all nine men had died from serious and multiple gun shot wounds. In his judgment of 24 May 1996, Mr Justice McCollum in the High Court refused to quash the coroner's decisions or the jury verdict. The families of Antony Hughes, Kevin Antony McKearney, Michael Gormley, Seamus Donnelly, Gerard O’Callaghan and Eugene Kelly filed civil proceedings against the Ministry of Defence.

The applicant’s stepfather was given a suspended sentence combined with seventy-five hours’ compulsory community service. He was ordered to pay the applicant damages in the amount of SEK 20,000. The Court of Appeal acquitted him on the counts of sexual molestation allegedly committed against the applicant. The court found it established that he had had a sexual intention in hiding the camera in the laundry basket and directing it at the part of the bathroom where it was usual to undress. The buzzing sound from the camera heard by the applicant strongly suggested that the camera was switched on and was actually recording. Whether a recording had actually been made, however, was unclear. A man filmed his sleeping girlfriend while he masturbated. The man was acquitted of sexual molestation because he had not intended his girlfriend to find out about the filming. The isolated act of filming was not a crime in itself, as in Swedish law there was no general prohibition against filming an individual without his or her consent. The Court of Appeal went on to point out that the act might, at least theoretically, have constituted the crime of attempted child pornography (försök till barnpornografibrott) considering the applicant’s age. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3684/07) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that the Swedish courts’ protracted custody proceedings, including their handling of his request for the return of his daughter under the Hague Convention, violated Articles 6, 8 and 13. The application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The proceedings relating to custody and rights of contact relate to the case of Mr Einar Strömblad and his daughter, N., who was born in Sweden in 2003. The Court of Appeal of Skåne and Blekinge upheld the lower court’s decision in full. It found that no circumstances had been presented which indicated the decision was not in the best interests of the child. N. should live with her mother, he wanted contact rights to be exercised on a regular basis according to a specific schedule. The parties were left to agree on where it would be best for N. and the applicant to meet. In this respect, the court emphasised that L. had a great responsibility to ensure that N. would be able to see the applicant. This decision was final on 13 December 2005. The applicant requested the District Court to change its interim decision, inter alia, in respect of N’s place of residence and the contact rights. He claimed that the interim decision in force had made it impossible for him to create meaningful contact with N., since it was too expensive to travel to Prague every other weekend. The Court of Appeal rejected the appeal, noting that it was not legally possible for it to decide where a child should live; it could only decide with whom. In 2006 the Social Council made an investigation concerning the custody of N. and contact to her, but the Court did not find the results satisfactory. In July 2007, the Court mandated a company, Access Borders SE, to investigate N.'s living conditions in the Czech Republic. L. took a number of procedural decisions, inter alia, rejecting L.’s request to have all documents in the case-file translated into Czech. The court decided that L. should have the sole custody of N. and granted the applicant a right of contact with N. four days in a row on a monthly basis, which should gradually be increased. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal, which refused leave to appeal on 29 September 2010. On 8 December 2010 the Supreme Court refused leave for the applicant to appeal against the decision of the District Court. The District Court held that both the applicant and L. were suitable parents. It concluded that the fact that N. had not seen her father for the last five years was to a large extent caused by L.'s behaviour. In June 2006 L. sent a notification of change of address to the Swedish Tax Authority (Skatteverket) on N.’s behalf. Since parents who have joint custody of a child need to agree on a change of. address for the child, L. agreed to move N. to Prague. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, claiming that the District Court should have focused on the actual removal of N. from Sweden by L. and not on the retention. In his view, the removal had been unlawful and the Hague Convention was therefore applicable. On 1 February 2007 the Supreme Court rejected the application. The applicant opposed the change of N’s place of residence in the Swedish population register (folkbokföringen) since he considered the removal of N. to be unlawful and the custody proceedings were still ongoing. The applicant appealed against the decision to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Skåne. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal. The case is still pending in the High Court of Justice of the Swedish Court of Appeal in Gothenburg, which could not hear the appeal due to the lack of a joint appeal by the applicant and L. The application has been adjourned pending further proceedings.

The prosecution is seeking to extradite the suspect to Germany to face charges of murder and attempted murder. The trial will be heard in May 2015, and if successful the suspect will be released from prison after serving his sentence. The accused has been charged with three counts of attempted murder and one count of aggravated assault. He also faces a charge of making false statements to a police officer in connection with the bombing.

The case is the first of its kind in Germany. The suspect was convicted of forgery in 1996. He was jailed again in 2000. The case is still pending in the German courts. The ECJ also ruled that international human rights law should be applied to all citizens, not just the rich and powerful. The ICC's ruling meant to protect the rights of all people, but also to protect human rights. It was the first time that the ICC had ruled on a human rights issue, and the first since the fall of the Second World War. The case was decided on the basis of the principle that human rights are human rights, and that they should be respected.

The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that the European Union must be reformed to make it more democratic. The decision was made after the European Parliament voted in favor of the EU being able to impose its laws on the EU. The vote was the first in the history of the Euro, and the first since the fall of the Second World War, when the EU was not able to win the right to a say in the matter.

The CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASEThe applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Maissau.Upon his baptism on 9 July 1994 he became a member of the Jehovah’s Witnesses in Austria. On 17 November 1994 the Lower Austrian Military Authority found that the applicant was fit to perform military service. The applicant appealed against an order allowing him to be exempted from military service under section 24(3) of the Military Service Act. He argued that he performed a function within the Jehovah’s Witnesses which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society. To restrict such a privilege to members of recognised religious societies was not objectively justified and was therefore in breach of the Federal Constitution. The Federal Minister for Defence (Bundesminister für Landesverteidigung) dismissed the applicant's appeal and confirmed the lower authority's decision. The Administrative Court (Verwaltungs-gerichtshof) dismissed his complaint on 26 March 1998. It noted that the applicant had solely complained about section 24 (3) in conjunction with the 1998 Act. In 1998 the Lower Austrian Military Authority issued another conscription order for an examination of the applicant’s fitness to perform military service. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court against the order. He submitted in particular that by virtue of the 1998 Act, the Jehovah's Witnesses had been granted the status of a “registered religious community’. The ten-year period for a successful application for recognition under the Recognition Act (Anerkennungsgesetz) lacked objective justification, he claimed. The Constitutional Court refused to deal with the complaint for lack of prospects of success. He then filed a request for recognition as a conscientious objector (Zivildiensterklärung), which was granted.

Lord Hoffmann says House of Lords should find that there is a general tort of invasion of privacy. He says it is not necessary to adopt a high level principle of privacy to comply with Article 8 of the Convention. The European Court is concerned only with whether English law provides an adequate remedy in a specific case in which it considers that there has been an invasion of. privacy contrary to Article 8 § 1 and not justifiable under Article 8. § 2, he writes. He adds that a merely negligent act should, contrary to general principle, give rise to a claim for damages for distress because it affects privacy rather than some other interest like bodily safety: compare Hicks v Chief Constable of the South Yorkshire Police. The coming into force of the Human Rights Act 1998 weakens the argument for saying that a general tort of invasion of privacy is needed to fill gaps in the existing remedies. If it is indeed the case that a person’s rights under Article 8 have been infringed by a public authority, he will have a statutory remedy. This is an area which requires a detailed approach which can be achieved only by legislation rather than the broad brush of common law principle. The creation of ageneral tort will pre-empt the controversial question of the extent, if any, to which the Convention requires the State to provide remedies for invasions of privacy by persons who are not public authorities.

Brentwood Borough Council installed a CCTV surveillance system in Brentwood in April 1994. The council's monitoring operator had a direct visual and audio link to the police so that if it was considered that an incident warranting police intervention was taking place, the images being captured could be switched through to police. In August 1995 the applicant was suffering from depression as a result of personal and family circumstances. On 20 August 1995 at 11.30 p.m. he walked alone down the high street towards a central junction in the centre of Brentwood with a kitchen knife in his hand and he attempted to commit suicide. He was unaware that a CCTV camera, mounted on the traffic island in front of the junction, filmed his movements. The CCTV footage later disclosed did not show the applicant cutting his wrists.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 44647/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant complained about the disclosure to the media of closed-circuit television footage, which resulted in images of himself being published and broadcast widely. He relied on Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required. The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the European Court of Human rights. It was decided that a hearing was not required. In August 1995 the applicant was suffering from depression as a result of personal and family circumstances. On 20 August 1995 at 11.30 p.m. he walked alone down the high street towards a central junction in the centre of Brentwood. He stopped at the junction and leaned over a railing facing the traffic with the knife in his hand. The police were notified by the CCTV operator and arrived. They took the knife from the applicant, gave him medical assistance and brought him to the police station. He was detained under the Mental Health Act 1983. His custody record refers to the self-inflicted injuries to his wrists on arrival and notes that he was examined and treated by a doctor after which he was released without charge. Anglia Television broadcast footage of the incident involving the applicant. The applicant's face was masked at the Council's oral request. However, that masking was later considered inadequate by the Independent Television Commission (see below) The applicant became aware that he had been filmed on CCTV and that footage had been released because a neighbour told his partner that the former had seen him on television. He did not take any action then as he was still suffering from severe depression. It appears that a number of people recognised the applicant in the CCTV footage. A letter of 25 April 1996 from the Yellow Advertiser opined that the applicant was not identifiable. The BBC agreed to mask the faces of people in a new series of ‘Crime Beat’ The series aired on Channel 4 in March and April 1996. The BBC did not say why the masks were needed. The producers of the series did not agree to the same requirement. The ban was lifted in July 1997 and the programme was broadcast again. The man was not identified in the final episode of the show, which aired on April 17, 1997. He has since appeared in a number of media appearances, including on BBC Radio 4 and BBC Radio 3. For confidential support call the Samaritans on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or see www.samaritans.org. The Broadcasting Standards Commission (BSC) upheld both of the applicant's complaints. The BSC noted that the BBC had already accepted that it had meant to mask the. applicant's image and that this had not been done in the trailer due to an oversight. The BBC was directed to broadcast a summary of the adjudication of the BSC with the episode of ‘Crime Beat’ on 12 June 1997. The ITC also found that section 2(2) and (5) of the Code had been breached and the decision of the ITC was published in its Programme Complaints and Interventions Report of June 1996. The applicant complained to the Press Complaints Commission (PCC) in respect of the articles published in the Yellow Advertiser in May 1996. The PCC rejected the applicant's complaint without a hearing and the decision was communicated to the applicant by letter dated 2 August 1996. On 23 May 1996 the applicant applied to the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Council's disclosure of the CCTV material arguing, inter alia, that that disclosure had no basis in law. On 26 June 1996 a single judge of the High court refused leave. The High Court granted leave on a renewed request and leave to amend the application to include a complaint that the disclosure was irrational, even if lawful. He argued that by failing to consult the police to see if he had been charged with a criminal offence, the Council had facilitated an unwarranted invasion of his privacy. The High Court judge had some sympathy with that submission but did not consider it correct in law. Unless and until there is a general right of privacy recognised by English law, reliance must be placed on effective guidance being issued by Codes of practice or otherwise, the judge said in his ruling on the case. In the. CCTV cameras in public places play an important role in both crime prevention and crime detection. In this case, the film footage showed a man walking in the High Street carrying a large knife in his hand. It did not show him attempting to commit suicide. It was plainly a potentially dangerous situation which the Council's monitoring employee quite properly put to the police. Anglia TV failed to mask the applicant's identity adequately. The BBC failed toMask the applicant’s identity at all in the trailers. Brentwood Borough Council were notified about that by the applicant, two days before the programme went out. They immediately contacted the BBC and received assurances that his image had been masked in the programme. In the event, unknown to the Council, it had not been adequately masked. An application to the High Court for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal was rejected. A subsequent leave application to a single judge of the Court of Appeal was also rejected. The Council was neither acting outside its statutory authority nor irrationally in making the film and photographs available to the media.

eval_texts: The case originated in two applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been denied fair trials, contrary to Article 6 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 10 September 2002, following a hearing on admissibility and the merits, the Court declared the applications admissible. On 1 July 2003 the Court decided to join the two applications (Rule 43 § 1) The application was brought by two United Kingdom nationals, Mr Martin John Edwards (“the first applicant”) and Mr Michael Lewis (‘the second applicant’) The applicants were represented by Mr P. Maynard, a lawyer practising in Tonbridge. The first applicant's defence was that at the time of his arrest he believed he was taking part in a transaction to sell stolen jewellery. He alleged that his participation had been organised by a man named Geoffrey Lerway. On 7 April 1995 the applicant was convicted in Snaresbrook Crown Court of possessing a Class A drug with intent to supply and was sentenced to nine years' imprisonment. The first applicant agreed to accompany Lerway to a public house where, at approximately 12.45 p.m., a red Jaguar car and a white van drew up. In the van was a briefcase containing 4.83 kilograms of 50% pure heroin. Of all the participants in the above transaction, only the applicant was arrested and charged. The applicant suspects that the other participants were undercover police officers or informers acting on police instructions, but their identities and status have never been revealed to him. At the time of the alleged dealings, Lerway was on bail to the Middlesex Crown Court in respect of a large scale conspiracy to supply cannabis. It was known to the applicant that Lerway had acted as a participating police informer in that case and it was further known that the police officers involved in the applicant's case had also investigated the conspiracy. The Government revealed for the first time that the material placed before the trial judge included information indicating that the applicant had been involved with heroin before the start of the undercover operation. The applicant denies any prior involvement in drug dealing. the public interest immunity evidence was not disclosed to the applicant during the domestic proceedings, either at first instance or on appeal. The defence made an application to the trial judge to exclude the evidence of Graham, on the basis that the applicant had been entrapped into committing the offence. The judge held that in the course of the ex parte application he had heard nothing and seen no material which would have assisted the defence in their argument that evidence should be excluded under section 78 on grounds of entrapment. Following his conviction the applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal on the ground, inter alia, that the judge had been wrong to refuse to order disclosure. The applicant was charged with possession of forged currency. He claimed he had been entrapped by undercover police officers. The judge refused to grant a stay or to order further disclosure of information. He also ruled that most of the information sought was subject to public interest immunity. The case against the applicant is expected to be heard at a later date. Patrick Shanaghan was shot dead by the RUC in Killen, Northern Ireland. The RUC discovered a car which they believed had been used by the people involved in the shooting. A forensic and fingerprint examination disclosed no evidence to connect it with any person suspected of the murder. Enquiries showed that the car had been recently bought for cash by unknown persons from a private vendor. Several suspects had been arrested and interviewed but no evidence of admission had been obtained from them. The inquest into the killing was opened on 26 March 1996, over four and a half years after the killing. The family of Patrick Shanaghan sought to introduce evidence in support of allegations that the R UC had prior knowledge that he was to be murdered. This consisted of evidence from a forensic science consultant who criticised the Ruc for not taking a plaster-cast of car tyre impressions.

The Shanaghan family home, which the applicant shared with her son, was searched sixteen times between 1985 and 1991. According to the applicant, sometimes the RUC would not even enter certain rooms indicating that the search was not a concerted effort to locate and seize illegal material but was carried out solely to harass the family. The applicant alleged that the behaviour of the police at the scene was not consonant with any concern for her son's life or proper police procedures. The Coroner accepted that the evidence should be admitted. The RUC Chief Constable applied for judicial review of those decisions. The High Court ruled that it was not germane to the question of how Patrick Shanaghan met his death. It said the evidence was relevant to the possible criticism of the standard of the police investigation and that that goes well beyond the scope of the inquiry of the coroner. The case was decided by a jury and a lawyer, with the R UC represented by counsel and a solicitor. Patrick Shanaghan died on 12 August 1991 from a bullet wound to the chest. The Coroner refused to admit in evidence statements made by Patrick Shanaghan to his solicitors. The applicant made a complaint about the conduct of the RUC at the scene of the shooting in denying Dr Stewart access to the body. This complaint was investigated by an assistant chief constable, under the supervision of the Independent Commission for Police Complaints (the ICPC) As a result, the Inspector concerned was given advice which was recorded in the Divisional Discipline Book. The RUC conducted further enquiries and reported to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) Inquiry into circumstances surrounding the murder was organised by family and friends after the conclusion of the inquest. The inquiry was conducted by the Castlederg-Aghyaran Justice Group and chaired by a retired United States Judge, Andrew Somers. The witnesses included family, local residents and friends of the deceased. Evidence was given alleging that police officers had frequently stopped Patrick Shanaghan in the street and issued threats. The judge concluded that the applicant had been murdered by the British Government and, more specifically, with the collusion of the RUC. The applicant claimed damages for loss and damage sustained by her and the estate of her son by reason, inter alia, of negligence.

Durham Prison Governor ex parte Hardial Singh [1984] 1 WLR 704 (see section on domestic law below), the Secretary of State cannot lawfully detain a person pending removal for longer than a reasonable period. In a judgment dated 14 November 2011 the Administrative Court dismissed the claim. It noted that in deciding whether or not there was a realistic prospect that deportation would take place within a reasonable time, the risk of absconding or re-offending were ‘of paramount importance’ The Administrative Court noted that the interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, was awaiting a lead judgment on returns to Mogadishu. The court also considered whether alternatives to detention could be used such as electronic tagging, monitoring by telephone and regular reporting. However, given the applicant’s history of absconding, it concluded that the alternatives would not have been sufficient and there was an absence of adequate assurances from the applicant. He also submitted that the detention was vitiated by two public law errors that bore directly on the decision to detain him. It accepted that although it was not possible to say when the proceedings before the Court would be concluded, there was nonetheless a reasonable prospect of removal being effected within a reasonable time. Court accepted that if the applicant were able to show that the decisions to maintain his detention were vitiated by public law he would succeed in establishing that the detention was unlawful and would have a claim of false imprisonment. Estonia, no. 10664/05, 8 October 2009 was authority for the proposition that the lack of a realistic prospect of deportation within a defined period rendered detention unlawful.

The applicant applied as a homeless person to Birmingham City Council for assistance in October 2006. The authority told the applicant that in its view the accommodation was suitable but following a review of that decision, which was determined in the applicant’s favour, they agreed to make her another offer. The applicant denied receiving the letter; instead, she claimed that she had to telephone the housing office to obtain the address and arrange the viewing appointment. She viewed the property on 19 March 2007 but declined the offer as she was not happy with the condition of the communal area. By reason of her rejection of its offer, pursuant to section 193 of the Housing Act its duty to her under Part VII of the 1996 Act had been discharged.

On 8 November 2006 the authority made the applicant an offer of accommodation which she refused because she was unhappy with the location. Following a review of that decision, which was determined in the applicant’s favour, they agreed to make her another offer. By letter dated 29 March 2007 the applicant notified the Council that she had not received an offer in writing and requested that the Council review its decision.

At each level, the grounds of appeal were that the decision taken by the Council’s Homelessness Review Officer had constituted a determination of the applicant's civil rights for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant submitted that the present case could be distinguished from that of Runa Begum because it concerned the simple question of a finding of primary fact rather than an evaluative judgment. The decision of the Officer had turned on the resolution of a question of disputed primary fact, involving no application of specialist knowledge.

The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. In doing so, it proceeded on the assumption that the case involved the determination of the applicant's civil rights for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant, a parent of two young children, is a homeless person in priority need of accommodation within the meaning of Part VII of the Housing Act 1996 (“the 1996 Act’). Birmingham City Council determined that the applicant was homeless, eligible for assistance and not intentionally homeless. The authority therefore accepted that it owed the applicant the “main housing duty” to provide accommodation to her and her family. On 7 November 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. The applicant viewed the property on 19 March 2007 but declined the offer as she was not happy with the condition of the communal area. By letter dated 21 March 2007 the Council notified the applicant that, by reason of her rejection of its offer, pursuant to section 193 of the Housing Act its duty to her under Part VII of the 1996 Act had been discharged. While the applicant’s case was pending before the review panel, a further offer of accommodation was made to her pursuant to a different scheme, namely the scheme for the provision of housing accommodation. She did not accept this offer. The applicant appealed to Birmingham County Court. The jurisdiction exercised by the County Court under section 204 was that of judicial review. In her grounds of appeal the applicant claimed that the Council had discharged its main housing duty. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal and then to the Supreme Court. At each level, the grounds of appeal were that the decision taken by the Council’s Homelessness Review Officer had constituted a determination of the applicant's civil rights. In Runa Begum the House of Lords found that judicial review provided ‘sufficiency of review’ for the purposes of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The judge noted that the only ground of appeal argued before him was that the letter of offer had failed to arrive. Although it was not specifically stated in the correspondence between the Council and the applicant, the judge appeared to consider whether or not the Council had discharged its duty under section 193(7) The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The applicant submitted that the present case could be distinguished from that of Runa Begum because it concerned the simple question of a finding of primary fact rather than an evaluative judgment. The House of Lords stressed that although the Officer had been called upon to resolve some disputed factual issues, these findings of fact were “only staging posts on the way to the much broader judgments” concerning local conditions and the availability of alternative accommodation. The public prosecutor asked for a list of all transactions concerning the applicant’s bank account from 1 January 2009 until that day. He based his request for information on Articles 161a, 51 and 70 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter ‘the CCP’) The public prosecutor did not order the bank to submit the information, but pointed to the obligations of witnesses set out in the CCP and the possible consequences of non‑compliance. The bank complied with both requests for information and submitted the information to the public prosecution office. The information received was analysed by the police and the public prosecutor. A list of fifty-three transactions deemed to be relevant was included in the investigation file as evidence. The applicant, as the lawyer of the accused, was granted access to the investigation file. From the case file he learned, for the first time, of the investigative measures concerning his own bank account. He asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to hand over to him all data received from the bank and destroy all related data at the public prosecution office. The applicant appealed against the decision. The court found that the investigation was lawful, that the bank had provided the information voluntarily, and that the documents could therefore only be returned to the bank. The Regional Court also decided to separate the documents in question from the general court file and only grant access to them if reasons proving sufficient interest were provided. The Hamm Court of Appeal confirmed the decision of the Regional Court. It found that the decision was proportionate and that the safeguards were not applicable. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint, without providing reasons (case no. 2 BvR 2268/12) The court ruled that the bank could not be considered a person assisting the applicant or a person involved in the professional activities of the applicant under Article 53a of the CCP (see paragraph 27 below). The judge concluded that the application was not valid as the bank had acted voluntarily and there had been sufficient suspicion for such an extensive analysis of his banking transactions.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 55287/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr John Edward Seton (“the applicant’s case was that he had been involved in a drug deal with Mr Pearman and Mr Bartlett. The applicant was convicted for the murder of a Mr Jon Bartlett and a co-defendant, Mr Lee Osborne, was tried and acquitted of assisting an offender. Mr Seton is currently detained at HMP Whitemoor and is represented before the Court by a lawyer practising in Croydon with Blackfords LLP. The applicant’s trial for the murder of Mr Bartlett started on 11 August 2008. At the trial it was accepted by the applicant that the real issue for the jury was whether he or Mr Pearman was the murderer. The defence objected to their admission in evidence but the judge ruled that they should be admitted. The judge stated that he was satisfied the evidence had extremely strong probative value as Mr PearMan ‘appeared to be expressing genuine outrage’ at being implicated in a murder in which he was in no way involved’. The admission of the phone calls was made pursuant to section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The judge indicated that Mr Pearman could not be called because he refused to give evidence. He noted that all the enquiries carried out by the police to date had confirmed his lack of involvement in the killing. The judge said that he did not consider that there would be any real prejudice to the applicant from the tapes being played. At trial, in addition to playing the tapes, the prosecution led evidence that the applicant and victim were known to each other and were both involved in drug dealing on a substantial scale. Items connected to drug dealing were recovered from Mr Bartlett’s home, one of which was a list of debts. The applicant appeared on this list and he was shown as owing the victim GBP 24,000. Witnesses also saw a white van in the vicinity of the shooting at the relevant time. The van had orange writing on the side, and was similar, if not identical, to the van that had been hired from AVA on the same date. Cell site evidence also demonstrated that the applicant and his co-accused were in the. vicinity of a road where the Vectra was found between 8.01 p.m. and 8.17 p.M. Phone evidence was led by the prosecution with the intention of showing that the. applicant’s mobile telephone was in the nearby area at the time of the murder. CCTV footage showed the applicant arriving in the white AVA van, wearing a baseball cap and making telephone calls to an associate at 1.47 a.m. The number dialled by the applicant was in the vicinity of the cell site covering the road where the Vectra was found. The prosecution’s case was that Mr Pearman, a man in his fifties, did not match the description of the gunman given by the eye-witnesses. The trial judge directed the jury as follows: “It is for you to decide what weight, if any, you attach to this evidence” Jury asked and were allowed to hear the tapes of Mr Pearman’s telephone calls again. On 26 August 2008, by a majority, the jury convicted the applicant of murder. He was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of thirty years. He appealed against conviction to the Court of Appeal. The appeal was initially considered and rejected by a single judge in February 2009. The application was renewed before the full court on 14 November 2009 and leave to appeal was granted. In doing so, the court found it to be arguable that the trial judge did not make sufficient investigations with regard to the production of Pearman. Full court heard the case and dismissed the appeal, reserving its judgment. The judgment was delivered on 12 March 2010. In relation to the tapes of Mr Pearman’s telephone calls, the court observed: “It is contended on behalf of the Appellant [the present applicant] that the tapes should not have been admitted without calling, or trying to call, Pearman to give evidence. ... The difficulty with this submission is the judge's finding of fact that Pearman would not give evidence” The judge considered this evidence to be important and to have strong probative value. We do not know whether the jury shared this view. The defence were able to say, as they did, that the statements were self-serving, made by a serious criminal. The Court of Appeal said that because of the lateness of the allegation, the telephone records for telephones used in the murder only went back to 23 April 2006. The judge’s decision was not marred by legal error; he took all relevant matters into account; and the decision to admit the recordings in evidence was not one that no judge could sensibly have made. For these reasons, we reject this ground of appeal. The safety of the conviction was also upheld. The evidence against the Appellant may have been circumstantial, but it was overwhelming. The police uncovered no evidence of any link between Pearman and either the Appeller or Bartlett, despite exhaustive enquiries. Evidence of Rita Willott was not challenged and was read at the trial. The weight of the evidence points clearly to a young man such as the Appellant rather than Pearman. He found that the complete absence of any procedural safeguards was a serious interference with the applicant’s Article 8 rights in that case, which called for particularly weighty reasons of public interest in justification. He considered that provided that a reasonable degree of protection was afforded by the domestic law, the Strasbourg Court would not interfere.

The court has a wide discretion under subsection (2) to impose conditions when making an order for suspension. The decision to provide the procedural safeguards introduced by the amendment of section 4 of the 1968 Act was within the margin of appreciation available to the United Kingdom. More generous safeguards could have been introduced (and they will be when the 1983 Act is amended) But the amendment goes far enough to meet the real thrust of the criticisms made in Connor.”

The applicant alleged that the Court of Appeal’s decision to dismiss her appeal and uphold the judgment making a possession order constituted an unjustified breach of her right to respect for her home and her family life and discriminated against her. The application was communicated to the Government on 3 May 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Cardiff. The Gypsy Council issued a notice of termination of licence to the applicant which expired on 6 February 2005. The Gypsy Council issued a claim for possession against the applicant and five members of her extended family, including her parents, in Neath Port Talbot County Court. In a witness statement lodged prior to the hearing, the applicant indicated that she intended to leave the site when her parents left. Judge Bidder QC gave a judgment on the preliminary issue of whether the applicant could challenge the making of a possession order in her case. He considered himself bound by the decision of the House of Lords in Kay and Price (see paragraph 42 below), which had examined the effect of this Court’s judgment in Connors v. the United Kingdom, no. 66746/01. The judge asked the parties to consider the date of 4th November 2006 being the date on which the [applicant’s] parents are required to leave. He was, however, satisfied that her son, who resided part of the time with her, had been involved in an incident on site in which he threatened someone with a gun, although it was not clear whether the gun had been real or merely an imitation. He made an order for possession against the applicant and suspended enforcement of the possession order against her until the same time and date. However, he was clear that the behaviour of [her son] on this site and his attitude towards the Farrows is such that I have to impose conditions on her continued possession. In November 2007 a bill which would amend the Mobile Homes Act 1983 (“the 1983 Act’) was introduced to Parliament. The effect of the proposed amendment was to allow a defendant in possession proceedings such as the applicant to challenge before the County Court the reasonableness of making a possession order. Lord Justice Dyson noted: “42. The significance of the amendment is that a claimant’s decision to seek possession does not involve summary eviction without judicial scrutiny of the justification of the claim to possession” On 12 December 2007 the applicant's appeal was dismissed. The real difference between the present case and Connors is not that the appellant had been in occupation for a shorter period than was the family in Connors ... On any view, the site was her home and had been for a substantial period of time. Dyson LJ concluded that since the amendment to the 1968 Act, it was difficult to conceive of a case in which a public law defence would succeed. He accepted that the vulnerable position of gypsies as a minority meant that “some special consideration should be given to their needs and different lifestyle” (citing Connors, § 83). He found that the main reason for the narrowing of the margin of appreciation in Connors was that the complete absence of any procedural safeguards was a serious interference with the applicant’s Article 8 rights. However, the precise scope of these safeguards was in his view, a matter for the national authorities to determine. He considered that provided that a reasonable degree of protection was afforded by the domestic law, the Strasbourg Court would not interfere. The court had no jurisdiction to take the reasons into account in deciding whether to order the occupant’s eviction. Absent a public law challenge, the occupant had no opportunity to challenge the reasons given by the local authority for seeking possession. The court has a wide discretion under subsection (2) to impose conditions when making an order for suspension. More generous safeguards could have been introduced (and they will be when the 1983 Act is amended) But the amendment goes far enough to meet the real thrust of the criticisms made in Connors. Dyson LJ found that the decision to provide the procedural safeguards introduced by the amendment of section 4 of the 1968 Act was within the margin of appreciation available to the United Kingdom. The decision was made on the basis of Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which covers the right to an old age pension. The Government of Germany said that this amount was sufficient to cover the cost of caring for the dancer. The allowance was set to expire on December 31, 1991. The court ruled that it was not possible to continue the payments without a change in the law. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of Germany. The applicant was arrested on 11 August 1995 on a public bus in the city of Århus. She had a dispute with a ticket inspector, who accused her of having travelled without a valid ticket. They requested that the applicant give her name and address, and since she refused, she was arrested at 9.30 p.m. In a letter of 14 September 1995 the Chief Constable provided his comments on the course of event, stating inter alia that she appeared hysterical and refused to reveal her identity. Chief Constable wrote to the applicant saying the length of her detention was due to her 'unwillingness to assist in replying to the question on which the police needed clarification' The applicant appealed to the Prosecutor General, who upheld the decision on 25 November 1997. Four police officers were heard as witnesses on 17 September 1998. The two police officers who made the arrest said the applicant twice had refused to give her name and address on their request, once after they had warned her that she would be arrested.

The Chief Constable of Viborg refused to grant the applicant compensation for the 12 hours she spent in a detention cell. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 52792/99) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case concerns the detention of the applicant from 9.30 p.m. on 11 August until 11 a.m on 12 August 1995. The applicant was represented before the Court by Mrs Hanne Gullitz, a lawyer practising in Århus. The Danish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Hans Klingenberg of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Co-Agent Ms Nina Holst-Christensen. The charge with the offence of refusing to reveal her identity was not followed up by an indictment. The applicant collapsed and was hospitalised for three days diagnosed with high blood pressure. The Chief Constable decided on the matter on 18 July 1996, and in so far as relevant his letter of the same day to the applicant reads as follows: “In connection with your previous complaint ... you received a ... letter of 14 September 1995 from Chief Superintendent HJH. [My] reply to your complaint... will not differ essentially from the content of [that letter]. However, in view of your relatively advanced age I find reason to regret that you were not, as promised, attended to by a doctor in connection withYour stay in the detention cell. This decision can be appealed against to the Ministry of Justice... The applicant did not appeal to the Ministry of Justice against the Chief Constable's decision. She complained against the decision to the Regional State Prosecutor in Viborg, who refused to grant her compensation on 6 February 1997. She appealed to the Prosecutor General, who upheld the decision on 25 November 1997. A court session was held on 26 June 1998, in which the applicant, represented by counsel, explained inter alia that she had refused to give her name to the ticket inspector partly because she was angry, partly because he already knew her. She alleged that the police did not question her or talk to her during the arrest, during the transportation to the police station, or after the arrival to the station. The City Court decided that the applicant was entitled to compensation in the amount of DKK 2,200. The prosecution appealed against the judgment to the High Court of Justice in Denmark. The applicant was detained for breaching section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act. The court found that there was no reason to extend the detention until the following day 11.00 a.m. They only succeeded around 10.45 a.M., whereupon she was released. A note of 9 July 1996 from the Chief of Police in Århus was submitted. It had been discussed in particular that the. applicant had not been attended to by a doctor in connection with her placement in the detention cell. The High Court gave judgment against the applicant in February 1999. The applicant's request of 24 February 1999 for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused by the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) on 25 May 1999. Under these circumstances, there is no basis for granting [the applicant] compensation pursuant to section 1018 a, subsection 1 of the administration of Justice Act. Moreover, as no circumstances has been established, which could provide a basis for giving compensation, [the court finds for the prosecution]’ The applicant was released as soon as she revealed her name and address.

The judge ruled that the charges were not substantiated, and the case was dismissed. The Court of Appeal found that the case had been resolved out of proportion to the charges against the applicant.

The 1994 Act provides for the making of a confiscation order in the event of a conviction for drug trafficking offences. On 5 June 2001 the applicant was found guilty of the offences charged. On 6 June 2001 he was sentenced to fourteen years’ imprisonment. He lodged an appeal against sentence, which was unsuccessful. In 2004 he lodged an out-of-time appeal against conviction. In early March, as a result of informal discussions between junior counsel for both sides regarding a case pending before the Court of Appeal, the 14 March 2001 date was vacated. The prosecution indicated its intention to proceed with the confiscation hearing on 20 May 2002, as planned. He was released on licence in October 1991 after serving the punitive part of his sentence.

In October 1990, having served the punitive part of his sentence, Mr Singh was released on licence. In March 1991 the Parole Board considered Mr Singh’s case, and on 21 March 1991 his licence was revoked by the Secretary of State on its recommendation. The reason given for his recall was not the alleged offences (which he denied) but that he had lied to and misled his supervising officers. Mr Singh has since been released from prison.

Prem Singh was sentenced to life in prison in 1973 for the murder of a 72-year-old woman. He was released on licence on 21 March 1991 on the recommendation of the Secretary of State for the Home Department. In March 1991 he was arrested and charged with a number of offences involving deception and using threatening behaviour. The reason for his recall was not the alleged offences (which he denied) but that he had failed to tell his supervising officers about them. On 27 August 1991 he received a more detailed explanation of his recall in a letter from the chief probation officer. Mr Singh is currently living in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, with his wife.

The Parole Board considered the applicant’s case on 27 August and 19 December 1991. It had before it a number of reports from the probation service and the police, none of which was disclosed to the applicant. The Board decided against recommending Mr Singh's immediate release. He was not told the reasons for this decision. The applicant then sought judicial review (see paragraph 47 below) of the two decisions. The court held that the applicant was entitled to a fresh consideration by the Parole board under the terms of the Criminal Justice Act 1991. Lord Justice Evans found, inter alia, that: “[Mr Singh] status is that of a person whose continueddetention is a breach of natural justice’

Mr Singh denied the accuracy of most of the allegations against him. He asked the Parole Board to review the merits of the revocation of his licence. The Board considered the applicant’s case on 27 August and 19 December 1991. It had before it a number of reports from the probation service and the police. None of which was disclosed to the applicant. On 30 July 1992 the Board again declined to recommend Mr Singh's release. The applicant then sought judicial review (see paragraph 47 below) of the two decisions. The court held that the applicant was entitled to a fresh consideration by the Paroles Board under the terms of the Criminal Justice Act 1991. Lord Justice Evans found, inter alia, that: “[Mr Singh] status is that of a person whose continueddetention has been a breach of natural justice’

Mr Singh was convicted of failing to provide accurate information about his circumstances to his supervising probation officer. He denied the accuracy of most of these allegations, and asked the Parole Board to review the merits of the revocation of his licence. Under section 62 (4) of the Criminal Justice Act 1967 the Board was empowered at this stage to take a binding decision for Mr Singh’s immediate release. On 19 December 1991 the Board decided against recommending Mr Singh's immediate release and he was not told the reasons for this decision. On 30 July 1992 the Board again declined to recommend his release. The applicant then sought judicial review (see paragraph 47 below) and the Divisional Court quashed the Board's decision. Lord Justice Evans found that the applicant was entitled to a fresh consideration by the Par parole board under the terms of section 39 (4).

Prem Singh was released from prison in 1994. He was not allowed to be present at the Parole Board review of his case. The Board decided not to recommend release. Mr Singh applied for judicial review of this decision, but he withdrew his application on or about 7 March 1994 because he had been offered an early review of the case by the Par parole board. He has appealed against the decision to release him. The appeal has now been rejected by the Court of Appeal. The case can be heard in the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom at the St James’s Park, London, on Tuesday 13th October 2013 at 9.30am.

Prem Singh was recalled to prison in March 1991. The Parole Board unanimously recommended his release subject to six months in a pre-release employment scheme. On 16 March 1995 the Divisional Court quashed the secretary's decision and ordered him to reconsider it. The court found, inter alia, that the correct test to be applied was whether Mr Singh constituted a danger to the “life or limb’ of the public. Mr Singh was released in October 1995.

Prem Singh was released from prison in October 1990. The decision was made under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), not the Vienna Convention on Economic and Social Rights (ICHR) The ECHR is a treaty between the European Union and the United States. The EU is the only country in the world that has a treaty with the ECHR. It is also the only nation that has the right to a bill of rights for parents of children who have been born after the age of two. The European Union does not have a law that says that children born after July 1, 1987 are entitled to a free hand in raising a child. The law only applies to children born before that date, not after it.

The European Court of Human Rights ruled that the provision of the European Convention on Human Rights was unconstitutional. It said that the right to a child's health care is a right of all people, not a right to be paid for by the state. The decision came in response to a complaint by the European Parliament and the European Commission. The European Court found that the amendment to the European Human Rights Act did not provide for the right for a child to be given health care. The ECHR ruled that there was no reason to believe that a child should not have access to the health care he or she was entitled to under the ECHR. It originated in an application (no. 19178/91) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a British citizen. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Court was constituted on 24 September 1994, in the presence of the Registrar, and the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 May 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Owen and Mr Pannick as well as replies to its questions. The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) TCPA (see paragraph 19 below). In accordance with the relevant legislation, an inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. The inspector was a Principal Housing and Planning Inspector, a civil servant and a member of the salaried staff of the Department of the Environment. The inspector had been appointed by the Secretary of State after approval of the Lord Chancellor. In his decision letter of 1 October 1990 the inspector rejected the appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g) but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture" The appeal on ground (a) fails. The appeal on grounds (b) and (g) also fail. The decision turns on the following main issues. Whether, if the development is inappropriate to the green belt, there are any special circumstances to justify the granting of planning permission. Whether the appeal buildings enhance or preserve the character or appearance of the conservation area. I shall also consider the effect of the development on the countryside surrounding the village. The Court of Appeal rules that the buildings should not be granted planning permission to be built on the site in Higher Whitley, Vale Royal Borough, Vale of Wight, Hertfordshire. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development under the General Development Order’. The applicant does not challenge the inspector’s decision under ground (b). Nevertheless paragraphs 14 and 15 of the decision letter, where he is still dealing with that ground, are relevant to the court's consideration of his decision on grounds (a) and (g) ... ... In my judgment ... it cannot be said that the inspector failed to take into account the fact that the applicant might, within his General. Development Order rights, erect buildings of a broadly similar nature. He addressed that very consideration in terms at paragraph 15. Inspector extended the applicant’s time for complying with the enforcement notice under ground (h) The question whether the alterations proposed to a building were, as he evidently thought, a ‘matter of cosmetics’ and would not meet the main objections was entirely a matter of planning judgment for him. It is to be remembered that, in order to stay within his General Development Order rights, the applicant must erect replacement buildings which, by their appearance and layout, could be considered as designed for the purposes of agriculture. If they are, their effect on the green belt, the countryside and the conservation area is irrelevant to the exercise of that right. I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.

The applicant alleged that her envisaged expulsion to Pakistan would breach Articles 8 and 6 of the convention. The case was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court on 25 November 2013. The application was made by Ms Farida Kathoon Khan (“the applicant”), on 19 June 2012. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mr H. J. Behrens, from the Federal Ministry of Justice. The court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant had been in a state of acute psychosis. A medical expert noted that she suffered from symptoms of schizophrenia and had diminished intelligence. She did not acknowledge her own psychological condition. The domestic court concluded that she remained a danger for the general public and a continuous stay in a psychiatric hospital had to be ordered. In November 2009 the applicant was granted privileges in the hospital, for example she was granted days of leave, which had not led to any complaints. She also started working full‑time in the laundry department of the clinic. This was possible due to her improved mental health. The Kassel Administrative Court refused the applicant’s action against the expulsion order. It upheld the decision that the applicant could be deported. The court ruled that the woman's family would not have to pay for her care if she was released. The court also ruled that there was no danger to the public health of the woman. The woman was allowed to stay with her family until the end of the year. She was then allowed to return to her work as a carer for the elderly in the town of Einsiedlitz. But she had to stay away from her family for the duration of her treatment. Her condition has since improved but she still has problems with her eyesight and her speech. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1497/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention. He was originally sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff (i.e. minimum term to be served before eligibility for release arose) of five years. Upon appeal, this was reduced to a sentence of imprisonment for public protection (“IPP” – see paragraphs 22-23 below) The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Chivers Solicitors, a firm of lawyers based in Bingley. The applicant’s tariff expired on 18 December 2008, by which time no Parole Board review had taken place. The applicant challenged, by way of judicial review proceedings, the delay in fixing a Parole board hearing. The hearing was eventually rescheduled for September 2009. The panel was not satisfied that sufficient evidence exists that your risk of sexual and/or violent offending has yet reduced to a level such that that risk can be safely managed out of closed conditions. They feared that there had been an underestimate of risk and insufficient attention to the sadistic elements of the offences in other assessments. They would therefore counsel against the formulaic approach in this case. The High Court handed down its judgment in the judicial review proceedings on 23 June 2009. The judge outlined the background to the applicant’s claim, as follows: “4. a breach, having regard in particular to the fact that the pre-tariff advisory opinion of the Parole Board had effectively made it clear there was no chance of release upon expiry of the tariff (see paragraph 7 above)” The judge considered that it followed “inevitably” from it that the panel, if asked, would not conceivably have directed the applicant's release. In fact it is common ground that Article 5(4) of the European Convention on Human Rights requires there to be a speedy hearing an independent judicial body. ‘Speedy’ does not indicate a particular period, and I accept entirely that it is fact sensitive. What may be required in a particular case may not be needed in another, depending upon the circumstances. In this case the cause has been the lack of man power in the Parole Board which has meant that it has been unable to provide the necessary panel. That is hardly surprising having regard to the importance of ensuring not only that those who should be released are released, but that those which should not be are not released.’ ‘It will take time for the position to be improved: that is inevitable. ... It may well be that it could be said that steps ought perhaps to have been taken at an earlier stage ... Nevertheless, that is historical, and as I say there is now a recognition’ The applicant had originally sought a mandatory order requiring that his case be heard in September. The judge agreed with the decision not to pursue the claim for such an order, observing that it would be inappropriate for an individual, seeking judicial review, to “jump the queue” at the expense of those who did not seek judicial review. The applicant’s legal representative accepted that it was “not of the greatest importance” whether a declaration was granted or not, because the terms of the judgment could show what the situation was. He decided: “In all the circumstances I do not think that it is necessary for me to make any formal declaration in the circumstances of this case” Judge says measures put in place to alleviate the problem will not have immediate effect. He says it is not now appropriate for any prisoner to take proceedings against the Parole Board alleging breaches of Article 5(4) Unless there are very special circumstances, something has gone badly wrong despite the new arrangements in that prisoner’s particular case. It will not be helpful, either to the prisoner or to the court, if claims are brought which in reality, because of the existing situation, are not likely to achieve any sensible redress and merely add to costs. The court cannot do the impossible. We cannot make orders which are only going to create difficulties for others and are not in any way desirable. The applicant was advised by his counsel that no appeal would be successful as the Court of Appeal would be bound to conclude that it could not prioritise any individual case. The Parole Board recommended that the applicant be moved to open conditions. The Secretary of State accepted the recommendation. The applicant was released in September 2009. He was released on bail in January 2010. He has been remanded in custody until the end of August 2014. He is currently serving a two-and-a-half-year suspended sentence for a drugs offence. The judge said that under. special circumstances, claims of this nature should now be discouraged. The court welcomes the steps that are clearly being taken now to. ensure that that situation does not continue.
