They also considered that she was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Alien Act, in force at the relevant time, since the applicant was 17 years old. Finally, it found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permitUnder section 9 c, section 9(2) of theAlien Act, under which she was applying for family reunification, she had not contacted the Immigration Service until August 2005. The applicant appealed against the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. The Immigration Service received a questionnaire from the applicant dated 12 July 2007 used for requests for exemption from the authorities revoking a residence permit. It stated, inter alia, that it had been the applicant’s parents’ decision that she should leave Denmark at the relevant time; that the applicant spoke Danish, but could not read or write the language; that she was very afraid and could not reside in her country of origin as there was unrest. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. Immigration Service brought case before Copenhagen City Court before which the case was decided on the documents submitted. On 25 April 2008 it found against the applicant. Decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret), henceforth the applicant remained in Kenya. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children under 15 years instead of under 18 years. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention as invoked by the applicant, and that the case would not have a different outcome. The applicant's parents sent her voluntarily to Kenya to live with family for an indefinite period. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. The applicant was advised to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien’s Act and the possibility of submitting an application for asylum under section 7 of the Aliens Act. The application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The High Court upheld the City Court's decision in October 2008, but said it could not review a final administrative decision of refusal of a residence permit under section 9c, subsection 1.

The applicant is four-limb deficient as a result of phocomelia due to thalidomide. The applicant alleges that she was forced to sleep in her wheelchair since the bed was hard and would have caused pain in her hips. She also alleges she was unable to use the toilet since it was higher than her wheelchair and therefore inaccessible. She was offered a hot drink and a meal but refused both. The doctor's note of his examination of the applicant at 12.35 a.m. states: “Patient complained of feeling cold, headache and queasy (no food since admission – offered but refused). Talking quite sensibly, not obviously hypothermia, seated in wheelchair. Tells me unable to lie flat and sleeps on sofa, sitting up, at home’ The applicant was not placed in a normal cell in New Hall, Wakefield, but was instead detained in the prison's health care centre. Her cell had a wider door for wheelchair access, handles for the disabled in the toilet recess and a hydraulic hospital bed. The applicant slept until 7 a.m., when she was moved to another cell and offered food and drink, which she refused. She was taken to New Hall Women's Prison and detained until the afternoon of 23 January 1995. On arrival at the prison the applicant completed a medical questionnaire. She stated that she had health worries but that they were ‘under control – takes it as it comes’ A 'continuous medical record' on the applicant was kept during her detention. The first entry, dated 21 January 1995, stated: ‘I asked duty Governor, Mr Ellis, to give permission for a battery charger for Adele's wheelchair to be brought in if we could arrange it’ The applicant alleged that on the evening of 21 January1995 she was lifted onto the toilet by a female prison officer, but was then left sitting on the toilet for over three hours until she agreed to allow a male nursing officer to clean her and help her off the toilet. The Government submitted that there was no medical condition to admit her to hospital with. Adele claimed she was exposed to two male prison nursing officers. The Government denied that these incidents occurred. The applicant was allowed to serve half her sentence under the Criminal Justice Act 1991. She needed catheterising due to urine retention before her release. Her medical record states that she was due for release this afternoon as soon as transport arrangements can be made. The remission provisions in sections 45 and 33 of the criminal justice Act 1991 meant that the applicant had only to serve three and a half days of her sentence. She was released on January 23, 1995, after serving half of the sentence imposed by the Supreme Court. She is currently serving a sentence of six months in prison. The applicant claimed to have suffered health problems for ten weeks as a result of her treatment in detention. She has not provided direct medical evidence in support of this claim. She was granted legal aid, limited to obtaining evidence and seeking counsel's opinion as to merits and quantum. Her counsel referred to the difficulties which the applicant was likely to face in proving that she had suffered the ill-treatment which she alleged, and that, even if successful, damages were not likely to exceed 3,000 pounds sterling. In the light of this advice, the applicant's legal aid certificate was discharged on 13 May 1996. She had some complaints about her sleeping arrangements. Said that Gv Ellis had said that she could sleep on a chair and have her cell door open all night.

The case was dismissed on the grounds that the suspicion concerning them had not been dispelled. The couple then sought compensation from the State for the pecuniary damage sustained on account of their detention. The Review Division (Ratskammer) of the Vienna Regional Court refused their compensation claims on the ground that, contrary to the requirements of section 2 (1) (b) of. the 1969 Act, the suspicion of them was not dispelled at the time of their arrest.

Johannes Werner, an Austrian national born in 1963, lives in Vienna. He was arrested on 15 May 1991 for fraudulently using a credit card which did not belong to him. On 1 July 1991 the police also arrested the applicant, who was suspected of having aided and abetted Mr and Mrs Hauser by forging the signature on the credit card. On 17 May 1991 they were detained pending trial. On 24 February 1992 the investigating judge at the Vienna Regional Court (Landesgericht) decided to discontinue the proceedings in the light of a graphologist’s finding that it was unlikely that the signatures on the payment slips for the purchases made with the stolen credit card were in Mr Werner's hand.

Mr Werner and Mr and Mrs Hauser appealed against that decision to the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) They asked the court to take further evidence and, in particular, to hear witnesses. No representative of the public prosecutor’s office attended the deliberations. The court ruled that suspicion must be dispelled sufficiently to establish that the detained person is not punishable, and cannot be prosecuted, on account of the conduct in respect of which his detention was ordered. Commission had produced various documents relating to the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. The applicant and Mr and Mrs Hauser sought compensation from the State for the pecuniary damage sustained on account of their detention. He had a system of fixed ideas and a missionary devotion to the implementation of his plans. His mental disturbances, combined with the further symptoms of aggressiveness, his cruelty and recklessness, entailed a high risk for third persons. The Supreme Court rejected the plea ofnullity as well as the appeal. The question of whether the victims had in fact been intimidated had been irrelevant. The applicant was found not to be dangerous due to his mental illness, but had a risk of further offences of the same kind.

The Regional Court found that his threats of murder were of such a nature as to intimidate third persons in general, and he had in fact intended to intimidate the persons concerned. Considering his mental illness, there was also a risk of further offences of the same kind. The Supreme Court, in its judgment, found that the rejection by the trial court of the applicant's requests for the taking of evidence did not impair the rights of the defence. It also confirmed the legal qualification of the offences committed by the applicant. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the applicant had failed to show any contradictions or shortcomings in the expert opinions which would be the only reason to justify a faculty opinion.

The applicant was convicted of the murder of Christopher Nugent and sentenced to life imprisonment. Nugent was the applicant’s business partner. He was shot and killed at their business premises on 15 December 1987 by Stephen Gray, who left the scene of the crime in a car driven by Gary Runham. Runham and Gray were arrested in January 1988 and the applicant was arrested in February 1988. The two alleged co-conspirators, who according to the prosecution had, together with the applicant, paid for Nugent to be murdered, were acquitted. The applicant complained to the Police Complaints Authority (PCA) about Suffolk Constabulary's refusal to disclose material evidence.

The applicant was born in 1946 and is currently detained in HM Prison Kingston, Portsmouth. He was convicted of the murder of Christopher Nugent and sentenced to life imprisonment in 1989. The Crown’s case was that the applicant had paid Runham and Gray 20,000 pounds sterling (GBP) to kill Nugent. The applicant claimed that he would have had no motive for killing Nugent, since the latter was himself involved in the fraudulent activities being perpetrated through the business. The two alleged co-conspirators, who according to the prosecution had, together with the applicant, paid for Nugent to be murdered, were acquitted. After investigation, in a letter of 30 October 1992, the PCA reported that it could not support any allegation of murder.

The applicant was convicted of the murder of Christopher Nugent and sentenced to life imprisonment. The applicant complained to the Police Complaints Authority (PCA) about Suffolk Constabulary’s refusal to disclose material evidence. After investigation, in a letter of 30 October 1992 to the applicant, the PCA reported that it could not support any allegation of a murder conspiracy. The two alleged co-conspirators, who according to the prosecution had, together with the applicant,. paid for Nugent to be murdered, were acquitted. The post-trial disclosure, however, found the applicant to be guilty of the crime and sentenced him to life in prison.

The Government says the evidence was not disclosed at first instance, but which was disclosed prior to the applicant’s appeal. The evidence came from the Holmes computer system used by the police officers conducting the murder inquiry to store and cross-reference all the information obtained in the course of the inquiry. The second category of evidence related to the parallel investigation into mortgage fraud by a number of people, including the applicant and Nugent. The Government said the evidence which was not disclosed at first instance, but which was disclosed prior to the applicant’s appeal, fell into two categories. The first type of evidence derived from the Holmes computer system used by the police officers conducting the murder inquiry to store and cross-reference all the information obtained in the course of the inquiry. The second category of evidence related to the parallel investigation into mortgage fraud by a number of people, including the applicant and Nugent. At an early stage, the prosecution decided to keep the murder and fraud investigations separate and that there was no duty under the Attorney-General’S Guidelines to disclose.

In July 1993, the applicant was told that there were seventeen boxes of hitherto undisclosed material. The Government submitted that, following the applicant’s conviction, and in the light of developments in the common-law duty of disclosure (see below), the prosecution reviewed their position and decided that the data stored on the Holmes computer system did amount to disclosable material. Prior to the applicant's appeal, therefore, the prosecution disclosed the messages and actions held by the police. Some 4,000 actions had been disclosed, one of which was referred to by the applicant in support of his appeal. The second category of evidence undisclosed at first instance related to the parallel investigation into mortgage fraud by a number of people, including the applicant and Nugent.

After the applicant’s conviction and the development of the common law, the prosecution reconsidered their decision and made full disclosure of the material obtained in the fraud inquiry. Counsel for the defence was in contact with the prosecution concerning possible further disclosure. Non-disclosure of evidence at trial, particularly evidence discovered in the parallel mortgage fraud investigation, was one of the applicant's grounds for appeal. The application was rejected and the applicant was convicted of murder in 1994. The appeal was heard before the Court of Appeal on 28 and 29 March 1994, and the appeal was denied. The applicant was awarded the right to appeal against the conviction and sentenced to life in prison.

The first applicant and Jakob Bachmayer concluded a contract on the transfer of the rights of the latter to the second applicant on 16 January 1991. They filed a complaint against this decision with the Administrative Court, which was dismissed on 8 October 1991. On 15 April 1992, after having held oral hearings in 1991 and 1992, the Regional Board dismissed the appeal against the Office of the Regional Governor of 27 June 1985 as regards “count 2” of the decision. The applicants filed a complaint against the Supreme Land Reform Board's decision to quash the Office of the Regional Governor's decision of 27 June 1985. On 6 June 2006 the Constitutional court declined to deal with the applicants' complaint for lack of prospects of success and, upon their request, transferred the case to the Administrative Court. The application was dismissed and the case was returned back to the Regional Govt. decision. The decision was quashed on 7 November 2005 and remitted the case back to that authority. The court held that the legal provision under review was not in accordance with the Federal Constitution and quashed the decision of the impugned authority of 4 December 2002.

Gaskin v. Liverpool City Council [1980] 1 WLR 1549 was a case about access to personal social services files. The High Court ruled that case records were private and confidential. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal. On 30 June 1982, the Sub-Committee’s recommendations, made available case records to ex-clients of the social services, subject to certain safeguards and restrictions relating in particular to medical and police information. Gaskin was to be allowed access to, and to make photocopies of, his case records, subject however to the exclusion of medical andPolice information. The decision was accordingly affirmed and leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused.

The Sub-Committee recommended making available case records to ex-clients of the social services, subject to certain safeguards and restrictions. On 1 April 1989 the Access to Personal Files (Social Services) Regulations 1989 came into force. These regulations impose upon social services departments a duty to give to any individual access to personal information held concerning him. According to the Government, the effect of Regulation 9 (3) is that, in future, case records will be compiled on the basis that the information contained therein is liable to be disclosed, except in so far as disclosure would be likely to reveal the identity of the informant or another third party. This is a very important service to which the interests - also very important - of the individual must, in my judgment, bow’ Gaskin v. Liverpool City Council [1980] 1 WLR 1549. The applicant was to be allowed access to, and to make photocopies of, his case records, subject however to the exclusion of medical and police information. Mr Lea, a dissenting member of the Sub-Committee, brought an action challenging the resolution and obtained an interlocutory court order preventing the City Council from implementing it until the trial of the action or until further order. The High Court’s decision was accordingly affirmed and leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused. The Court of Appeal unanimously dismissed the appeal. The High Court granted the Attorney General leave to apply for judicial review of the resolution of 26 January 1983 as amended. Mr Lea brought a legal action against the Council which the Council discontinued on 13 May 1983. On 29 June 1983 the local authority confirmed a further resolution to the effect that the resolution would be implemented as from 1 September 1983. The Department of Health and Social Security issued Circular LAC (Local Authority Circular) (83) 14 to local authorities and health authorities pursuant to section 7 of the Local Authority Social Services Act 1970. The circular set out the principles governing the disclosure of information in social services case records to persons who were the subject of the records. Liverpool City Council blocked the release of 352 documents. The Attorney General withdrew his application for judicial review. The Director of Social Services of Liverpool City Council wrote to the applicant’s solicitors in the following terms: “I would wish to be as helpful as possible to you, but at the end of the day suspect that we may have genuine differences of opinion.” The court heard how the City Council refused to release 65 documents supplied by 19 persons who had consented to their disclosure. The City Council then refused to disclose the documents, saying they were ‘unprofessional’ and ‘in the public interest’ ‘I regret I do not feel able to help you further. last analysis, for the provider of information, retrospectively collected, to release or refuse to release, in their absolute discretion, the information supplied from the ‘confidential’ embargo originally accorded to it. The reasons for releasing or not releasing are irrelevant whether they are good, bad or indifferent.’ ‘The Government, the effect of Regulation 9 (3) is that, in future, case records will be compiled on the basis that the information contained therein is liable to be disclosed, except in so far as disclosure would be likely to reveal the identity of the informant or another third party' ‘By virtue of section 2 (4) of the Access to Personal Files Act 1987, the 1989 Regulations apply only to information recorded after 1 April 1989. On 23 January 1986, the Commission declared admissible the applicant’s complaint concerning the continuing refusal of Liverpool City Council to give him access to his case records. In its report of 13 November 1987 (Article 31) (art. 31), the Commission concluded, by six votes to six, with a casting vote by the acting President, that there had been a violation of Article 8 (art., 8) of the Convention by the procedures and decisions which resulted in the refusal to allow the applicant access to the file. The full text of the Commission's opinion and of the partly dissenting opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to the present judgment.

The applicants challenged that decision before the courts. Both requested an interlocutory injunction to stop their deportation. The applicants had gone to school in Norway, had friends and acquaintances there and were mastering the Norwegian language, both oral and written. The City Court further observed that in Norway the applicants had close relatives – uncles and aunts – and had lived with these since 2001. The applicant alleged that he had not had a fair trial as there were insufficient guarantees to exclude legitimate doubt regarding the independence and impartiality of the tribunal which tried him on criminal charges. The Crown case was that D.G. had been summoned to the scene by the applicant and another co-accused, M.H., using a mobile telephone belonging to D.M. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the Crown's evidence regarding the alleged phone calls came from a number of sources. Crown case involved video recordings from closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras near the scene. From a combination of video recordings and mobile telephone records for M.H.'s telephone, the Crown contended that the applicant could be seen making certain calls. There was also eye witness evidence of him making at least one of the critical calls. The applicant's case at trial was that he had made no calls on M. H.'s mobile telephone. However, he said that he was a drug dealer using his own telephone and that the calls were made for his own criminal purposes and were nothing to do with the summoning of D.G. The jury asked to be shown the video evidence again on the second day of their deliberations. The judge agreed that the recordings could be taken into the jury room and played there by the jury if required. The prosecution argued that the jury should be able to watch the video on their own. The jury retired and the case was adjourned until the next day. The case was decided in favour of the applicant by a majority verdict of not guilty. The verdict was quashed on appeal by the Court of Appeal in March 2013. The trial continued until the end of the trial in April 2013. Supreme Court observed that as the “fair trial” guarantee under Article 6 was distinct from the ‘reasonable-time’ guarantee it had to be approached separately. The court concluded that the correct “starting point” in the applicants’ proceedings was 5 April 2005 and the case was remitted to the Appeal Court. The Appeal Court dismissed the first applicant’s appeal against conviction and sentence on 27 March 2014, and the second applicant‘s appeal on 19 June 2014. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated as he was not permitted to build a second house on his property. He complained about the length of the related proceedings before the administrative authorities and courts and also about the refusal of the Supreme Administrative Court to hold an oral hearing. By a decision of 30 November 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The applicant’s late father had applied on 13 June 1989 to the Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) of Lund for tentative approval (förhandsbesked) of a plan to divide Humanisten 1 and build a new one-family house. The purpose of such an approval, issued under Chapter 8, section 34 of the 1987 Act, was to give a property owner who was planning a building project the possibility to obtain an advance assessment of whether the planned measures may be permitted at all. In assessing an application for a building permit made within two years after the grant of tentative approval, the Building committee was bound by the determinations made in that approval. On 15 April 1992 the Building Committee granted the applicant a tentative approval of a plan to divide the plot – Humanisten 1 – and to build a new one-family house. Several of the applicant’s neighbours opposed the measure with reference to the special character of the neighbourhood. The Land Survey recommended that the property plan be repealed in order to facilitate a division of the property enabling the applicant to construct a new house on the resulting new plot. A new property plan would not be required; repeal of the existing plan would be sufficient and the division would be consistent with the detailed development plan and be suitable for its purpose. It appears that those proceedings were at a standstill until January 1997 (see section 4 below) The Government quashed the Board’s decision to repeal the property plan. for Humanisten 1. The Government observe that the entire block has long been occupied by buildings in accordance with the city plan and plot divisions. .... The Government find that the suitability of the intended change of the property and the development conditions within the block ought to be examined through a new detailed development plan for the area in which the size and situation of the buildings can also be regulated to a sufficient extent. In view of this and everything else which has emerged in the case, the Government find. that the decision to repealed the propertyPlan should be quashed. Supreme Administrative Court ruled that the Government’s decision was not unlawful and confirmed it. Court held that the decision to quash the lower instances’ decisions regarding the property plan does not conflict with any legal rule in the manner claimed by the applicant. The application for re-opening of the case was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court on 10 April 2002. The adoption of a new detailed development plan and related proceedings was also ruled not unlawful. The Court found that the adoption of the plan was within the scope of jurisdiction of the authorities in planning matters. It should therefore be upheld. The case was dismissed on the grounds that the case could be examined and decided without holding an oral hearing. The applicant appealed against the decision to the Board, which on 18 January 1999 upheld the Council’s decision. The applicant made a further appeal to the Government, which was rejected on 23 June 2004. The Board found that the public interest in protecting the cultural heritage of the neighbourhood outweighed the applicant's private interest. It quashed the Building Committee's 15 April 1992 decision on the grounds that the tentative approval was contrary to the existing property plan and detailed development plan. The neighbours claimed that, although they were affected by the decision, the Committee had failed to hear them in the case or inform them about the decision. In a decision of 31 March 2000, the Board first found. that the neighbours were entitled to appeal against the tentative approving and was satisfied that they had done so within the required time-limit. 10 February 1999 to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Skåne. In September he asked the court to give priority to the case. In November 2000 the applicant appealed against both judgments to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten), in Gothenburg. On 15 September 2004 the Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal in both cases. In separate proceedings in 1997, 1997, the applicant sought a declaratory judgment establishing liability in relation to the building permit. The applicant was awarded a settlement of £2.2 million in 1998. He was also awarded a further £1.5 million in 1999. The applicant requested the District Court (tingsrätten) of Lund to declare that the Municipality of Lund was liable to pay him compensation for both actual and potential damage caused. The District Court found that the Building Committee had disregarded a clear and unambiguous provision in the 1987 Act. Since the applicable plans did not allow the grant of a building permit and since an amendment to the plan could not be a condition attached to a tentative approval, such approval should not have been granted. The Municipality appealed to the Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of Skåne and Blekinge. By judgment of 13 October 1998 the Court declared that the municipality was liable for the applicant's damages. In 2001 the applicant instituted civil proceedings against the Municipality requesting compensation in an amount of SEK 3,000,000 for the damage he had suffered due to the refusal to grant him the building permit. The Municipality contested the request. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal, which on 23 May 2005 refused the applicant leave to appeal. The Supreme Court of Sweden dismissed the applicant's appeal against the decision in May 2005. The case is still pending in the District Court of Lund and the applicant is seeking compensation for the damages he claims he has suffered as a result of the refusal of a building permit to build a new house.

The applicant was born in 1937 and lives in Mank/Austria. He had been a farmer and the owner of a farm. His sister argued that the farm was a hereditary one (Erbhof) within the meaning of the Agricultural Succession Act 1958 (Anerbengesetz) The applicant and his sister filed an application to be appointed as its principal heir. But the court found that it did not qualify as a hereditary farm because it could not provide a living for five adults as required under the applicable law. The court dismissed the appeals and upheld the Regional Court's finding. The other heirs appealed but the appeal was dismissed on 18 October 1990.

Mr Lustig-Prean joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. On 27 April 1983 he became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy. He was asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject) He was also asked about his current relationship and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality. He then confirmed that he was homosexual, acknowledging that he had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years.

Four men were discharged from the army on the sole ground of sexual orientation. The High Court dismissed the application for judicial review on 7 June 1995. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” But he concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. The primary decision was for him and the secondary judgment amounted to asking whether a reasonable Minister could have reasonably made that primary judgment.

In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. The only countries operating a blanket ban were Turkey and Luxembourg (and, possibly, Portugal and Greece) , Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals to serve in their armed forces. On 3 November 1995 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court. of Appeal agreed). The more substantial the interference with human rights, the more the court will require by way of justification before it is satisfied that the decision is reasonable in the sense outlined above.

Only Turkey and Luxembourg operated a blanket ban on homosexuals in the armed forces. The applicants in the judicial review proceedings had argued that the Ministry of Defence’s position was “bereft of factual evidence” The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal on 3 November 1995. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court of appeal agreed). He considered that the court may not interfere with the exercise of an administrative discretion on substantive grounds save where the court is satisfied that the decision is unreasonable in the sense that it is beyond the range of responses open to a reasonable decision- maker. But in judging whether the decision-maker has exceeded this margin of appreciation the human rights context is important.

eval_texts: The case originated in two applications against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from the Royal Navy on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Government, represented by Mr M. Eaton and, subsequently, by Mr C. Whomersley, both Agents, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, submitted their observations on 17 October 1997. The Commission decided to adjourn the applications pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice (“ECJ”) pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome. The High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998) The applications fall to be examined by the Court in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 of the Protocol No. 11. On 4 May 1999 the President of the Chamber decided to grant Mr Lustig-Prean legal aid. The hearing in this case took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 May 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Eadie, Counsel, Ms J. Betteley, Ms. Pfieffer, Advisers. The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. He became a midshipman in the executive branch of the navy in 1983. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. The applicant was interviewed on 13 June 1994 by personnel from the service police about his sexual orientation for approximately 20 minutes. He was asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject) and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality. He then confirmed that he was homosexual, acknowledging that he had been a practising homosexual since his teenage years. The application was denied. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy in 1989. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. On 16 December 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. He left the ship ‘with a well-deserved reputation for outstanding professional ability and admirable personal qualities’ The applicant’s report dated 27 November 1992 noted that he displayed potential in a number of areas essential to good leadership. In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) and consequently he spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. He was then called for interview by the service police. The applicant immediately confirmed his homosexuality, later clarifying that he first had “niggling doubts” about hissexual orientation approximately two and a half years previously. The interview was suspended pending the search. During the search, slides (of himself, his partner and some of his service friends) and personal postcards were seized. The service police report completed after the applicant’s interview included several internal documents where it was noted that the applicant, in openly declaring his homosexuality and his relationship with a civilian, had effectively disposed “of any immediate potential security concern” For that reason, it was considered in the report that “no cause was identified for conducting a security interview with Beckett” That report also accepted that a case for fraudulent entry into the armed forces would be inappropriate given the date when the applicant had discovered his homosexuality. The applicants’ judicial review proceedings (R.C. v. Ministry of Defence, ex parte Smith and Others 2 Weeky Law Reports 305) The High Court dismissed the application for judicial review. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. He noted that the cases illustrated the hardships resulting from the absolute policy against homosexuals in the armed forces. All four of the applicants had exemplary service records, some with reports written in glowing terms. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” The case was heard at the Royal Courts of Justice in London. For confidential support call the Samaritans in the UK on 08457 90 90 90, visit a local Samaritans branch or click here for details. Simon Brown LJ also found that the Equal Treatment Directive was not applicable to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. He also observed that the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, Israel, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, Austria and the Netherlands permitted homosexuals into the armed forces. A brief analysis of the Convention’s case-law led the judge to comment that he strongly suspected that, as far as the United Kingdom's obligations were concerned, the days of the policy were numbered. It followed that the applications had to be rejected “ albeit with hesitation and regret”. In exercising merely a secondary judgment, this Court is bound to act with some reticence. Our approach must reflect, not overlook, where responsibility ultimately lies for the defence of the realm. In August 1995 a consultation paper was circulated by the Ministry of Defence to ‘management’ levels in the armed forces relating to the policy against homosexuals in those forces. It was indicated that the case was likely to progress to the European courts and that the applicants in the judicial review proceedings had argued that the Ministry’s position was “bereft of factual evidence’ On 3 November 1995 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicants’ appeal. The Master of the Rolls, Sir Thomas Bingham, delivered the main judgment (with which the two other judges of the Court. of Appeal agreed) He considered that the court may not interfere with the exercise of an administrative discretion on substantive grounds save where the court is satisfied that the decision is unreasonable in the sense that it is beyond the range of responses open to a reasonable decision- maker. Master of the Rolls: Court must not shrink from its fundamental duty to ‘do right to all manner of people’ He noted that the case concerned innate qualities of a very personal kind, that the decisions of which the applicants complained had had a profound effect on their careers and prospects and that the applicants’ rights as human beings were very much in issue. However, he concluded that the policy could not be considered “irrational” at the time the applicants were discharged from the armed forces, finding that the threshold of irrationality was “a high one” and that it had not been crossed in this case. “It is, inevitably, common ground that the United Kingdom’s obligation, binding in international law, to respect and ensure compliance with [Article 8 of the Convention] is not”. Henry LJ of the Court of Appeal agreed with the judgment of the Master of the Rolls and, in particular, with the latter’s approach to the irrationality test and with his view on the inability of the court to resolve Convention issues. He questioned the utility of a debate as to the likely fate of the ‘longstanding’ policy of the Ministry of Defence before the European Court of Human Rights with which the primary adjudicating role on the Convention lay. Thorpe LJ agreed with both preceding judgments and with the views expressed on the rationality test to be applied and on its application in the particular case. He also found that the Equal Treatment Directive did not apply to complaints in relation to sexual orientation. In December 1995 Mr Lustig-Prean issued proceedings in the Industrial Tribunal claiming unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination contrary to the Sexual Discrimination Act 1975. Those proceedings were adjourned pending the above-described application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords. In December 1997 Mr Beckett also issued proceedings claiming sexual discrimination. In the light of subsequent decisions of the ECJ and of the domestic courts, the second applicant subsequently requested the withdrawal of those proceedings which were, on 27 August 1998, dismissed by the Industrial tribunal. The applicants’ Industrial Tribunal proceedings were dismissed on 25 April 1996. The appeals committee of the Appeals Committee of the House. of Lords refused leave to Appeal to the Lords on 19 March 1996.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 247/07) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained about the length of civil proceedings and lack of an effective remedy under Articles 6 and 13. The Government and the applicant each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits. The Court ruled in favour of the Government. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Denmark, which handed down its ruling on December 25, 2010. The decision was published by the European Court of Human rights and Human Rights, on December 28, 2010, and is available for download from the court's website.

The case originated in an application (no. 247/07) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained about the length of civil proceedings and lack of an effective remedy under Articles 6 and 13 of the convention. The Danish Government (the Government) were represented by their Agent, Mrs Nina Holst-Christensen of the Ministry of Justice. The Government and the applicant each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits. The Court accepted the Government's observations and ruled in favour of the Government on the merits of the application.

The Government and the applicant each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits. The case was decided in favour of the applicant and the Government on the merits, and the case was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 11 June 2011. The decision was made by the majority of the nine-person panel of the Court, which was made up of judges from the European Court of Justice and the Supreme Court.

The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in Lyngby. She underwent two cystoscopic examinations at the County Hospital in Gentofte in May 1992. She also underwent a diagnostic laparoscopic examination in October 1992. The applicant alleges malpractice on the part of the consultant who performed the examinations. The Patient Insurance Association (Patientforsikringen) refused to grant her compensation. Copenhagen County (Københavns Amt) was ordered to acknowledge its liability in damages for the injuries allegedly incurred in connection with the examinations carried out at Gent ofte County Hospital. On appeal, on 20 January 2000 the Patient Injury Appeals Board (Patientskadeankenævnet) upheld the Patient insurance Association’s decision.

The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in Lyngby. She underwent two cystoscopic examinations at the County Hospital in Gentofte in 1992. The applicant’s insurance company filed a grievance with the National Patients’ Complaints Board (Sundhedsvæsenets Patientklagenævn) The latter found against her by decision of 28 September 1995. On appeal, on 20 January 2000 the Patient Injury Appeals Board (Patientskadeankenævnet), upheld the Patient Insurance Association's decision. She changed counsel at least five times during the proceedings before the High Court, which ended on 13 November 2002.

The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in Lyngby. She received treatment at the Urological Unit of the County Hospital in Glostrup. In May 1992 she underwent two cystoscopic examinations. In October 1992, she underwent a diagnostic laparoscopic examination. In June 1995, alleging malpractice, the applicant instituted civil proceedings before the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) She requested that Copenhagen County be ordered to acknowledge its liability in damages for the injuries allegedly incurred in connection with the examinations carried out at Gentofte County Hospital. The applicant’s insurance company, acting on her behalf, filed a grievance with the National Patients’ Complaints Board.

The applicant asked the Medico-Legal Council for an expert opinion. The questions were discussed and approved by the High Court. The case has been adjourned five times since the start in 1996. Her request was granted and the patients’ injury appeals board submitted its writ of defense on 3 October 2000. On 22 December 2000 the Medical Council issued their opinion on 4 August 2000. The application was dismissed on 5 June 2001. The applicant appealed against her dismissal, but her appeal was refused on 5 May 2000. In October 2000 the proceedings were adjourned for two months.

The High Court agreed to allow the applicant to submit nine questions to the Medico-Legal Council. The High Court decided on the wording of the questions and re‑submitted the matter to theMedico‑Legal Council on 14 May 2001. The applicant was granted approximately one month to consider the further procedure. On 21 February 2002 the applicant’s fifth lawyer informed the High Court that she was resigning from the case. The trial was scheduled to take place on 9 and 11 September 2002 but was postponed after the defendant objected to the scheduling and brought the issue before the Leave to Appeal Board without success. On 28 May 2002 the applicant’s sixth counsel submitted a pleading containing a notice of evidence for the trial as well as new exhibits. During the subsequent months the final pleadings were submitted. The trial was held on 9 and 11 November 2002.
